pronunciation.approximation: MAATH — a long, open 'ah', held like the a of 'father', closing on the soft voiceless th of English 'thin'. One syllable; the whole weight of the name sits on the length of the vowel and the hush at the end.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Math (Math uab Mathonwy) is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The standard etymology derives the name from Proto-Celtic *matu- 'bear' — compare Old Irish math 'bear' (attested in the compound mathgamain), the Irish name Mathgen borne by the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish Matugenos 'bear-born'. The father's name, Mathonwy, is built on the same root, and the handbooks treat the bear-derivation as the best-supported reading.

domains.title: Magic, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Math
domains.lead: In the celtic tradition, Math governed magic, kingship. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.name: The Wand of Office
cards.desc: Math's hutlath — the magic wand that tested Arianrhod, turned his nephews into beasts for three years, and helped fashion a woman out of flowers.

cards.name: The Footholder's Geas
cards.desc: The strange condition of his kingship: Math could not live except with his feet in the lap of a virgin, unless the turmoil of war released him.

cards.name: The Threefold Sentence
cards.desc: His justice wore animal skins: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy spent a year each as deer, boars, and wolves — and their beast-children were baptized at his court.

cards.name: The Flower Bride
cards.desc: With Gwydion he took oak, broom, and meadowsweet and made Blodeuwedd — the wife no earthly race could supply for the nephew fated to have none.

symbols.name: The magic wand (hutlath)
symbols.meaning: The rod of transformation and testing — proof, punishment, and creation carried in one length of wood

symbols.name: The virgin's lap
symbols.meaning: The footholder's office — the geas that bound the king's life to an untouched maiden, save in time of war

symbols.name: Goewin ferch Pebin
symbols.meaning: The footholder of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, wronged in the king's own house and made his queen in redress

symbols.name: The swine of Annwfn
symbols.meaning: The otherworld herd whose engineered theft gave Gwydion his war — the first pigs in Wales, and the pretext that broke the geas

symbols.name: Hyddwn, Hychddwn, and Bleiddwn
symbols.meaning: Stag, pig, and wolf — the three beast-sons of the punished brothers, restored to human shape and baptized

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet
symbols.meaning: The three flowers Math and Gwydion wove into Blodeuwedd, the bride made by craft

mythology.lead: Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi — the branch that bears his name: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His rule hangs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live except with his feet in a virgin's lap, unless war calls him out — and around that geas the whole plot turns: the theft of the swine, the wrong to Goewin, the justice of the three animal years, and the making of a bride from flowers.

myths.title: The Geas of the Footholder
myths.text:
Math son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and the tale's first fact about him is the condition of his life: except when the turmoil of war prevented it, he could not live unless his feet lay in the lap of a virgin. The office of footholder went to Goewin daughter of Pebin of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, the fairest maiden of her generation; and while Math kept the lap, his sister's sons Gwydion and Gilfaethwy ruled the realm in his stead.

The arrangement is neither joke nor luxury: it is the Fourth Branch's picture of sacral kingship, a rule whose life is bound by taboo. When Gilfaethwy sickened with desire for Goewin, Gwydion read the geas like a statute. The king may leave the lap for one thing only — war. Therefore there would be a war.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
Pryderi of Dyfed held the hobeu, the swine sent him from Annwfn by its king Arawn — the first pigs ever brought to Wales. Gwydion went south in the guise of a poet, conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, traded the day's glamour for the herd, and was gone before the illusion faded. Pryderi mustered and came north, and Math led Gwynedd out to meet him — out of the lap, exactly as the condition required.

At the parley Pryderi demanded single combat, for it was because of him that the hosts had come; at the maenor of Penardd Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed gave hostages and went home under tribute. But while Math marched, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin in the king's own chamber. The war had only ever been the key, and the lap the lock.

myths.title: The Queen and the Three Skins
myths.text:
Goewin would not hide what had been done to her, and Math's first act was redress: he took her as his wife and made her queen, so that the disgrace should not fall on her. Then came judgment. He struck Gwydion and Gilfaethwy with his magic wand into a stag and a hind, and sent them into the wild for a year; when they returned with a fawn, he made them a boar and a sow for the second year, and a wolf and a she-wolf for the third.

Each year's offspring — Hyddwn, Hychddwn Hir, and Bleiddwn — the king took in beast-shape, restored to human form, baptized, and raised. After the third year he struck the brothers back into men: they had had punishment enough, he said, and been greatly shamed, and he received them back into honour. It is the most exact justice in the Mabinogi — transformation as sentence, a year for each skin of the debt, and restoration without residue.

myths.title: The Stepping over the Wand
myths.text:
A new footholder was needed, and Gwydion named his own sister, Arianrhod daughter of Dôn. Math put the question plainly — was she a virgin? — and set the test: step over my wand. As she stepped, she dropped a sturdy yellow-haired boy. Math had him baptized at once and named him Dylan, and the boy made straight for the sea and took its nature, Dylan son of Wave.

And as Arianrhod turned to go, she dropped 'something small', which Gwydion swept up and hid in a chest at the foot of his bed — the boy who would be Lleu Llaw Gyffes. The wand that punishes is also the wand that proves: in one gesture the age of footholders ended and the age of the Children of Dôn began.

myths.title: The Bride Made of Flowers
myths.text:
Arianrhod, shamed before the court, laid her tynghedau on the boy: he should have no name until she named him, no arms until she armed him, and no wife of any race then on earth. Gwydion's craft undid the first two; for the third there was no earthly answer, and it was Math who joined him in making one. The two enchanters took their wands and, from the flowers of the oak, the broom, and the meadowsweet, fashioned the fairest and most beautiful maiden anyone had seen, baptized her, and named her Blodeuwedd — and gave her to Lleu.

The tale records no death for Math. The branch ends with Lleu restored and avenged, ruling Gwynedd after, and the old king simply withdraws from the record — the stillness at the centre to the last.

lore.syncretism: Math is the Welsh reflex of a pan-Celtic institution: the sacral king whose rule is bound by taboo. Irish tradition gives the condition its clearest grammar — the gessi of kings, the network of prohibitions whose slow breaking dooms Conaire Mór in Togail Bruidne Da Derga — and Math's footholder geas is the same machinery in Welsh dress, a kingship valid only while its condition holds. Mac Cana reads the Children of Dôn as the Welsh counterpart of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the name itself crosses the water on its own root: Cath Maige Tuired names Mathgen as the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish epigraphy attests Matugenos — both 'bear-born', from the *matu- that names the king and his father. Within the Mabinogi the root echoes across the branches: [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the Irish king of the Second Branch, carries the same Math- element. His closest kin are the members of his own house — his sister [[don|Dôn]]'s children, above all [[gwydion|Gwydion]], whose plots the geas licences and whose punishments the king's wand performs — and the co-made bride [[blodeuwedd|Blodeuwedd]], his one act of creation.
lore.culturalLegacy: Math's afterlife is quieter than his nephews', but the Fourth Branch carried him far. In the twentieth century the branch was remade twice over: Evangeline Walton's The Virgin and the Swine (1936) retells his story as a tragedy of old religion and new, with the geas and the three animal years as its moral engine, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain made Math son of Mathonwy the aged High King of Prydain for a generation of young readers — the geas laid aside, the grave authority kept. Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) drew its haunting from the Blodeuwedd strand that Math's wand set in motion, the branch repeating itself down the generations of a Welsh valley. In scholarship he stands at the centre of the Mabinogi industry: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi fixed the text, Sioned Davies's Oxford translation carries it to the world's readers, and Mac Cana's and Koch's handbooks treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose, with the footholder geas among the most-discussed cruxes in Celtic studies.
lore.extendedMeditation: Math is the proof that a story's most powerful figure can be its stillest. He does not trick, march, or seduce; he sits, and the sitting is the kingship — feet in a maiden's lap, the realm held by nephews, the whole arrangement waiting for someone to notice that war is the one door out of the geas. What makes him great is what he does after the door is used against him: redress before revenge, a wronged girl made queen, a sentence fitted exactly to the crime and limited exactly to it, and then — the rarest thing in any mythology of punishment — restoration without residue. His wand does everything the tale needs: it tests, it transforms, it creates. But its deepest work is juridical. Math is the king whose magic is law and whose law has a measure — three years, three skins, and the account closed — and whose stillness is not weakness but the condition of rule itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Math (Math uab Mathonwy), in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain math.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

lore.archaeology: Math is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), the two codices in which the Fourth Branch survives. The epigraphic witness belongs to the root rather than the man: Gaulish personal names such as Matugenos, 'bear-born', attest the *matu- element in the onomastics of the continental Celts. The tale's own geography is real Gwynedd terrain — Dôl Pebin in Arfon, where Goewin's father held his land — and the branch's southern war-road runs to the maenor of Penardd, where Pryderi fell.
